[![Facebook](https://alextimes.com/wp-content/plugins/social-media-feather/synved-social/image/social/regular/96x96/facebook.png)](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Falextimes.com%2Ffeatured-news%2Ffairfax-county-data-center-substation-hearing-postponed-to-december%2F&t=Fairfax%20County%20data%20center%20substation%20hearing%20postponed%20to%20December&s=100&p[url]=https%3A%2F%2Falextimes.com%2Ffeatured-news%2Ffairfax-county-data-center-substation-hearing-postponed-to-december%2F&p[images][0]=https%3A%2F%2Falextimes.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F09%2FData-Center-Residents-4-scaled.jpg&p[title]=Fairfax%20County%20data%20center%20substation%20hearing%20postponed%20to%20December "Share on Facebook") [![twitter](https://alextimes.com/wp-content/plugins/social-media-feather/synved-social/image/social/regular/96x96/twitter.png)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Falextimes.com%2Ffeatured-news%2Ffairfax-county-data-center-substation-hearing-postponed-to-december%2F&text=Hey%2C%20check%20this%20out%21 "Share on Twitter") [![mail](https://alextimes.com/wp-content/plugins/social-media-feather/synved-social/image/social/regular/96x96/mail.png)](mailto:?subject=Fairfax%20County%20data%20center%20substation%20hearing%20postponed%20to%20December&body=Hey%2C%20check%20this%20out%21:%20https%3A%2F%2Falextimes.com%2Ffeatured-news%2Ffairfax-county-data-center-substation-hearing-postponed-to-december%2F "Share by email")

**By Sydney Kodama \| skodama@alextimes.com**

Alexandria and Fairfax residents are preparing to speak out against a proposed data center substation in Fairfax County, next to the City of Alexandria.

Residents in opposition to the Edsall Road data center project who identified the public hearing on the Dominion Energy substation as their only avenue to give input will now have to wait: Dominion has successfully requested to delay a Fairfax County Planning Commission public hearing on the substation from Sept. 24 to Dec. 2.

The Save Bren Mar coalition, which opposes the data center project, announced the delay in a Sunday email blast and update to its [website](https://sites.google.com/view/savebrenmar/home). Bren Mar Park is in Fairfax County next to Plaza 500, the proposed site for the substation and data center.

![](https://alextimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Plaza500Neighborhoods-1_08_29_26_KrisPark-10-scaled.jpg)Watergate at Landmark condominiums are in the City of Alexandria across Edsall Road from the planned data center campus. (PHOTO/KRIS PARK)

“While \[Dominion Energy officially cites\] the need to submit ‘additional materials,’ this is transparently a stall tactic meant to quiet public outcry,” the coalition’s website states.

The delay has been confirmed by the Fairfax County Planning Commission’s [agenda](https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/planningcommission/sites/planningcommission/files/Assets/calendar/2026/9.24.26.pdf) for Sept. 24.

Greg Mathe, director of electric transmission engagement and permitting for Dominion Energy, said in an interview with the Times that Dominion Energy requested the delay so its staff can respond to questions ahead of the public hearing.

“These additional questions – for instance, ‘What is the noise decibel level at the boundaries? What’s the lighting or \[electromagnetic field\] emissions?’ – are not typical questions \[for this type of application\], and so answers to those questions were not prepared at that time, Mathe said.

“Specifically those three questions are ones that we are \[gathering data for\] now, and we want to be responsive, even though they’re sort of outside the normal questioning in that process,” he continued.

Residents were unable to give input on the [data center campus](https://plus.fairfaxcounty.gov/CitizenAccess/Cap/CapDetail.aspx?Module=Site&capID1=REC24&capID2=00000&capID3=009BE&agencyCode=FFX) planned for the Edsall Road site earlier in the process because it was approved by the county by-right, or automatically, because Fairfax County allows data centers in industrial zones.

Alexandria Planning & Zoning Director Paul Stoddard [said](https://alextimes.com/local-news/local-government/alexandrians-oppose-fairfax-data-center-substation/) in an interview with the Times that a data center in the City of Alexandria would have to be approved by City Council, and would not be approved by-right.

The proposed electric substation would support two data center buildings at the 34-acre Plaza 500 site on Edsall Road in Fairfax County, adjacent to the City of Alexandria. Starwood Capital Group, the investment firm responsible for the project, plans for the first of the two buildings to take up 226,469 square feet and be 75 feet tall, according to the [Washington Business Journal](https://www.bizjournals.com/washington/news/2026/07/21/plaza-500-south-starwood-alexandria-edsall.html).

“The data center is something that they’ve already approved, and so we have an obligation to serve, and we have an obligation to furnish reliable power for both that customer as well as the surrounding community, which will be served out of this new substation,” Mathe said.

The substation would be approximately 67 feet from the closest homes in Fairfax County, according to the Save Bren Mar coalition website, and [less than 1,000 feet](https://alextimes.com/local-news/local-government/alexandrians-oppose-fairfax-data-center-substation/) from nearby homes in the City of Alexandria.

Tyler Ray, founder of the Save Bren Mar coalition, said in an interview with the Times that residents hope their opposition to the substation will impact the larger data center project.

“Data centers need power in order to be able to operate, and unless Dominion is able to demonstrate that this specific project is in alignment with the county Comprehensive Plan … they won’t be able to build the substation where they are proposing to build it,” Ray said. “Without that, I’m not quite sure what their options are.”

The Dec. 2 public hearing is a “2232” public hearing, which means that the public hearing on this item is about whether the substation is in line with the county’s Comprehensive Plan.

“This process determines if the general or approximate location, character and extent are in substantial accord with the Fairfax County Comprehensive Plan,” [the county’s website states](https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/planning-development/public-facilities-review/process).

Within the Comprehensive Plan, a map made to guide future development lists Lincolnia, the area where the data center campus would sit, as a Community Business Center.

“\[For Community Business Centers,\] redevelopment should encourage a mix of uses focused around a core area of higher intensity, such as a town center or main street in a pedestrian-oriented setting,” the [Comprehensive Plan](https://online.encodeplus.com/regs/fairfaxcounty-va-ap/doc-viewer.aspx?secid=657#secid-656) states. “Transitions in intensity and compatible land uses should protect surrounding stable residential neighborhoods.”

The surrounding area is identified as a suburban neighborhood by the map.

In preparation for the public hearing, residents have gathered more than 1,700 signatures in an open letter asking Gov. Abigail Spanberger to oppose the project, hosted community meetings with local elected officials and shared flyers to spread the word.

Starwood is represented by public relations firm H/Advisors. Mark Detlor, senior vice president at H/Advisors, declined an interview with the Times and subsequently provided a statement from Melody Neil, Starwood Digital Ventures spokesperson.

“The planned redevelopment of the Plaza 500 site is an essential opportunity for Fairfax County to replace what was once an active, industrial site with a less obtrusive investment that secures the County’s future and enables its growth, Neil said in the statement.

“SDV is continuing to work closely with Dominion Energy and Fairfax County to ensure plans for the Edsall Road substation, a public good subsidized by SDV, are community-conscious and low-impact,” Neil continued.

Ray said the Save Bren Mar coalition last met with Starwood in 2022 and last requested to meet with the firm about one year ago.

“Despite their public claims otherwise that they’re working and continually engaging with the community, we have not met with them since 2022 – not because we haven’t asked, but because they’ve refused,” Ray said. “… I think after them refusing to meet with us for multiple years, at a certain point you just kind of give up, knowing that the answer is going to be no.”

![](https://alextimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Data-Center-Residents-3-scaled.jpg)The substation and two data center buildings are planned for the data center campus. (PHOTO/KRIS PARK)

Ray said the coalition has been reaching more and more City of Alexandria residents – many had not heard about the proposed project near their homes until recently.

“There’s been a few Alexandria residents who have been involved and aware for a significant amount of time, but … although this took place on the border … Dominion and the developer and others were not required \[to\] do any sort of outreach to Alexandria residents to let them know that this project was occurring, Ray said.

“As a result, not due to any fault of their own, they were really shut out of being able to contribute in this process,” he continued.

He said the Alexandria community has mostly only been involved for about a month, since a July 28 Mason District Land Use Committee meeting at which Dominion Energy presented on the substation.

Angela Cannon, Alexandria and Watergate at Landmark resident, said in an interview with the Times she first learned about the project from her condominium association’s newsletter and decided to attend the July meeting.

“I met lots of my neighbors \[at the meeting\] and lots of other people, and I learned quite a bit about the history of this – that the reason I had never heard of this … it seems like \[the developers weren’t\] notifying anyone in Alexandria,” she said.

Cannon said she began passing out flyers opposing the substation at Charles E. Beatley, Jr. Central Library to spread the word after reading more about the impacts of data centers.

“I had heard about data centers on the news, and I always felt sorry for people who were living next to them because of the noise,” she said. “But the more I start to read about them, the more I realize it’s way beyond the noise.

“It’s pollution that these diesel generators give off … it’s the way they take water out of the ground that we all use … and of course the electricity,” Cannon continued. “It’s everything about it. It’s just so antithetical to a neighborhood.”

Cannon said she had planned to retire across the street from the planned data center project but is concerned about the pollution, including noise pollution, the site could produce.

“I know I’m not going to be able to put up with that kind of noise, and I have a pet,” she said. “I have no idea what it’s going to do to my pet either. I don’t think I can live with constant noise, and I definitely don’t want my asthma to get worse.”

Haskell Taub, an Alexandria and Watergate at Landmark resident, said in an interview with the Times that he learned about the data center project through his condominium association’s newsletter as well.

He said he’s concerned that he did not learn about the project earlier and that Dominion has delayed the public hearing.

“There’s fear now that this is a huge delaying tactic, and they’re waiting for after the election and people have forgotten about the problem, but my feeling is that there’s going to be a blue wave at the election, and the data center is becoming such a national issue that Dominion is going to be forced to rethink this project,” Taub said. “But I think the secrecy of this thing is very upsetting.”

Adrienne Fikes is the executive director of Alexandria People’s Assembly, an organization which teaches the local community to advocate on issues impacting them.

The Alexandria People’s Assembly hosted an Aug. 15 panel on the impact the data center project could have on Alexandria’s West End neighborhood. Fikes said in an interview with the Times that her organization led a conversation about how to advocate against the project.

“This is the cry of the community, that this substation is the only point within this process where the voices of the people are being heard,” Fikes said. “And since we teach people to advocate, we’re building community and empowering advocacy so people can use their voice in civic engagement.”

Renee Grebe is the Northern Virginia conservation advocate for Nature Forward, a regional organization that advocates for residents to protect the local environment. She said in an interview with the Times that she’s been following data center developments across the region and is particularly concerned about the plans for Edsall Road.

“If you don’t put the substation there, then you don’t need these transmission lines \[carrying energy from the substation\] … along the stream,” Grebe explained. “Turkeycock Run is the stream to the west, and you have to cut down trees to put power lines because you don’t want the trees to interfere with the wires, and so you have this undermining of a ‘Resource Protection Area.’”

An [environmental parcel report](https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/gisapps/ParcelInfoReportJade/EnvironmentalReport.aspx?ParcelID=0812%2001%20%200007) generated by the county’s website for 6295 Edsall Road, the address of the proposed data center project, identifies 79% – or approximately 26.3 acres – of the site as lying on a “Resource Protection Area.”

Resource Protection Areas are “corridors of environmentally sensitive land that lie alongside or near the shorelines of streams, rivers and other waterways,” according to the report.

“That’s 100 feet to either side of a stream that’s supposed to be protected in Fairfax County, but utilities are exempt from that state code,” Grebe said.

Dominion Energy’s [website](https://www.dominionenergy.com/edsall) notes that construction of the substation “may have limited environmental impacts” and “access to surrounding neighborhoods may be impacted.”

“When you take those trees down at the Turkeycock Run on the west, you reduce the buffers from those residents who are now going to be next to this enormous building,” Grebe said.

Mathe said Dominion is planning to place buffers around the substation.

“As far as replantings, a lot of that is going to happen around the landscaping that we put around the substation,” he said.

Mathe and Grebe both noted that the transmission line – which will prompt tree removal – serving the substation has been approved by the Virginia State Corporation Commission, which regulates utilities.

Mathe also said that the SCC accepted public comments before approving the new transmission line.

“We notified folks in the surrounding area. … During the state corporation commission process, there \[were\] about 40 written public comments,” Mathe said. “The SCC also held a local public hearing in December of 2024 … so there were many opportunities for the public to be engaged both in our development process as well as the \[SCC\] process.”

Grebe’s concerns are not only environmental in nature.

The data center campus is approximately one mile from the nearest Metro stop, Van Dorn Street.

Grebe pointed to Loudoun Gateway – “the loneliest Metro stop,” according to a 2024 article from [The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2024/12/27/least-used-metro-loudoun-gateway/) – as an example of a Metro stop near a data center.

Author Joe Heim described Loudoun Gateway as the leastused Metro stop and argued that the low residential density near the stop “isn’t how it was supposed to be.”

Loudoun County has more than 250 data centers – making the county and Northern Virginia home to the highest concentration of data centers in the world, according to the [Northern Virginia Regional Commission](https://www.novaregion.org/1598/Data-Centers).

Grebe pointed out that Metro stops are built with the intention of serving nearby residents – not data centers.

“Certainly in Fairfax where you’re so close to D.C., we don’t want to see data centers, \[which are\] essentially a social dead zone,” she said. “… It’s not something that drives an activated space.”

With three months to go until the scheduled public hearing on the substation, the Save Bren Mar coalition’s next gathering is Sept. 16, when they will educate residents on how to submit impactful public comments ahead of the public hearing.

Mathe said Dominion Energy is planning an open house on the substation in the fall.

“There may be some confusion around our application and the site development there, and so we want to make sure that we come back out to the community and clear up any confusion,” he said.

Ray emphasized that the Save Bren Mar coalition is advocating against the entire data center campus, not just the substation.

“It really is about the data center campus as a whole,” he said. “It’s just kind of right now through the lens of the substation because the public has been shut out of the process otherwise. … We’re going to make the most of it and make sure that the public shows up to make sure their voices are heard.”
